name: alist-cons
summary: Puts a new (key . datum) pair on the front of an association list, without looking at what is already there.
explanation: alist-cons is exactly (cons (cons key datum) alist), and knowing that is knowing the whole verb. It does not search, it does not replace, and it does not complain about a key that is already present. The new pair goes on the front and the old alist becomes its tail, unchanged and shared. That is the point, not an oversight: because assq, assv and assoc all return the FIRST match, putting a pair on the front shadows every earlier pair with the same key, and removing the front pair uncovers the old one again. So an association list built with alist-cons behaves like a stack of scopes -- push to override, pop to restore -- which is why interpreters have used the shape for their environments since the 1960s. The cost is that the list grows even when the key repeats: three overrides of the same setting leave four pairs, not one. If you want the list to stay short, alist-delete the key first, or accept the growth and pay for it in lookup time.

examples.note: ((b . 2) (a . 1)) -- the new pair goes on the front, the old list becomes the tail.

examples.code:
(define base '((a . 1) (b . 2)))
(define shadowed (alist-cons 'a 9 base))
(display (list 'new shadowed 'lookup (cdr (assq 'a shadowed)) 'base base))
(newline)
examples.note: (new ((a . 9) (a . 1) (b . 2)) lookup 9 base ((a . 1) (b . 2))) -- both pairs for a survive, assq finds the front one, and base is untouched.

examples.code:
(define (alist-from-pairs ps)
  (fold (lambda (p acc) (alist-cons (car p) (cdr p) acc)) '() ps))
(display (alist-from-pairs '((x . 1) (y . 2) (z . 3))))
(newline)
examples.note: ((z . 3) (y . 2) (x . 1)) -- folding alist-cons over pairs builds an alist in reverse order, because each new pair lands on the front.

caveats: It does not replace. (alist-cons 'a 9 '((a . 1))) is ((a . 9) (a . 1)) -- two pairs, not one. Lookup gives 9 because assq stops at the first match, but length grew.
Repeated overrides of the same key grow the list without bound. If the alist is long-lived and hot, alist-delete the key before consing, or use a hash table.
The tail is SHARED, not copied: (cdr (alist-cons k v al)) is eq? to al. Mutating the old alist changes the new one too. alist-copy is the verb that breaks the sharing.
It takes key and datum as two separate arguments, not one pair. (alist-cons '(a . 1) '((b . 2))) is an arity error, and writing (alist-cons (car p) (cdr p) acc) is the idiom for feeding it a pair.
Which lookup verb you pair it with decides which keys can shadow: assq compares with eq?, assv with eqv?, assoc with equal?. A string key consed on will not be found by assq.
usecases: Pushing a scope frame onto an interpreter environment, where the innermost binding must win.
Layering user settings over defaults so the defaults stay intact and can be restored by dropping the front pairs.
Building an association list from a stream of key/value events with a single fold.

learn.concept: An association list is a stack, and shadowing is what you get for free when lookup returns the first match.
learn.progression: Cons a pair onto an alist by hand, then notice alist-cons is that same expression named. Then cons a DUPLICATE key on and see that assq answers the new value while length answers 2. That gap between what lookup sees and what the list holds is the whole idea of scope.

row-2-audit.eng-program:
(define defaults '((volume . 5) (fullscreen . #f)))
(define (override key value settings) (alist-cons key value settings))
(define user (override 'volume 9 defaults))
(display (list 'volume (cdr (assq 'volume user)) 'fullscreen (cdr (assq 'fullscreen user)) 'depth (length user)))
(newline)
row-2-audit.math-program:
(define (extend f x y) (alist-cons x y f))
(define f2 (extend (extend '() 1 1) 2 4))
(display (list 'domain (map car f2) 'image (map cdr f2) 'size (length f2)))
(newline)
row-2-audit.cs-program:
(define layered (alist-cons 'k 'new '((k . old))))
(display (list 'list layered 'assq-sees (cdr (assq 'k layered)) 'length (length layered) 'delete-instead (alist-delete 'k '((k . old)))))
(newline)
row-2-audit.problem: A settings screen has to apply a user's choice over a default without destroying the default. Candidates: alist-cons (one call, O(1), default survives underneath and can be restored by dropping the front), alist-delete then cons (keeps the list short but throws the default away), a hash table set! (fast lookup but the old value is gone and the whole structure is now mutable), rebuilding the list with map (O(n) and needs a branch for the key-not-present case). alist-cons is right when the OLD value still matters; it is wrong when it does not, because then you are just leaking pairs.
row-2-audit.explanation: eng: overriding volume leaves fullscreen reachable and the depth counter shows the default is still down there. math: the same verb read as extending a finite map one point at a time, where the domain is the keys and the image is the data. cs: the honest picture of what consing a duplicate key does -- assq answers the new value, length answers 2, and alist-delete is shown next to it as the verb that actually removes.
row-2-audit.meta: Why alist-cons and not alist-delete-then-cons: the row is about which tool an operator picks, and the deciding question is whether the previous value is garbage or history. Settings stacks want history. Caches do not.
row-2-audit.eng: Overriding by pushing means undo is just dropping the front pair -- no copy of the defaults has to be kept anywhere else.
row-2-audit.math: Extending a finite map by one point is a total operation; nothing has to be checked first, because a new point simply masks any old one at the same argument.
row-2-audit.cs: The gap between what assq reports and what length reports is the leak. It is harmless for a settings stack and fatal for a loop that overrides the same key a million times.

row-3-dimension.setup: Putting a new labelled value in front of the old ones, so that whoever looks first sees the new one and the old one is still underneath.

rungs.domain: logging temperature readings from named stations
rungs.code:
(define (log-reading station celsius log) (alist-cons station celsius log))
(define readings (log-reading 'roof 21 (log-reading 'cellar 12 '())))
(display (list 'latest-station (caar readings) 'latest-celsius (cdar readings) 'entries (length readings)))
(newline)

rungs.domain: a lexical environment, where an inner binding hides an outer one of the same name
rungs.code:
(define (bind name value env) (alist-cons name value env))
(define (lookup name env)
  (let ((hit (assq name env)))
    (if hit (cdr hit) 'unbound)))
(define env (bind 'x 10 (bind 'y 20 (bind 'x 1 '()))))
(display (list 'x (lookup 'x env) 'y (lookup 'y env) 'z (lookup 'z env)))
(newline)

row-3-dimension.explanation: As bare structure it is a cons of a cons -- a pair on the front of a list of pairs, and nothing more. Applied to measured data it becomes an append-only log: each reading is stamped with the station that produced it, the newest is at the front, and nothing is overwritten, so the history is the list. Lifted to a lexical environment it becomes scope: bind x to 1, then to 10, and lookup answers 10 because assq stops at the first match, while the 1 waits underneath for the inner frame to be dropped. Same three-argument call every time; what changes is whether the front position means newest, or means innermost.
row-3-dimension.meta: The ladder is really about what 'first' is taken to mean. Structurally it means leftmost. In a log it means most recent. In an environment it means most local. The verb never learns the difference -- the reader supplies it.
row-3-dimension.eng: An append-only log and a settings stack are the same data structure read from different ends. Choosing alist-cons commits you to newest-in-front.
row-3-dimension.math: Function extension by a new point, iterated. The composite map is defined at every argument any layer defined, and the outermost layer wins ties.
row-3-dimension.cs: This is how environments were represented before hash tables were cheap, and it is still how small interpreters do it -- because pushing a frame costs one cons and popping it costs one cdr.

row-4-proof.eng-program:
(define (grows-by-one? key value al)
  (and (= (length (alist-cons key value al)) (+ 1 (length al)))
       (equal? (car (alist-cons key value al)) (cons key value))))
(display (map (lambda (c) (apply grows-by-one? c))
              (list (list 'a 1 '()) (list 'b 2 '((a . 1))) (list 'a 9 '((a . 1))) (list 'z 0 '((a . 1) (b . 2))))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.math-program:
(define (shadows? key value al)
  (eq? value (cdr (assq key (alist-cons key value al)))))
(display (map (lambda (c) (apply shadows? c))
              (list (list 'a 'one '()) (list 'a 'two '((a . old))) (list 'z 'three '((a . 1) (z . 2))) (list 'q 'four '((q . 1) (q . 2))))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.cs-program:
(define (tail-is-the-original? key value al)
  (eq? (cdr (alist-cons key value al)) al))
(define shared '((a . 1) (b . 2)))
(display (map (lambda (al) (tail-is-the-original? 'k 'v al))
              (list '() '((a . 1)) shared (alist-cons 'x 0 shared))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.claim: alist-cons always makes the list exactly one pair longer and puts (key . datum) at the front; the pushed key always shadows any earlier one under assq; and the tail of the result is the original list itself, not a copy.
row-4-proof.invariant: For all key k, datum v and alist a. length(alist-cons k v a) = 1 + length(a); car(alist-cons k v a) = (k . v); cdr(assq k (alist-cons k v a)) = v; and cdr(alist-cons k v a) is eq? to a
row-4-proof.meta: Three separate claims because three separate things could break. What would falsify them: a length that stayed the same (meaning it replaced), an assq that found the older pair (meaning it appended instead of prepended), or a tail that was a fresh copy (meaning it was O(n) and safe against mutation -- it is neither). The duplicate-key cases in each list are the ones that matter; the empty list is there because it is where cheap implementations forget to allocate.
row-4-proof.eng: The length law is what tells you the cost. Every override is another pair, forever, unless something deletes.
row-4-proof.math: Shadowing is the statement that the extension of a map at a point overrides rather than conflicts. Without it, extension would be a partial operation with a precondition.
row-4-proof.cs: eq? on the tail proves there is no copy. That makes the operation constant-time and makes the old alist an alias, both of which are consequences of the same single cons.

row-5-emergence.eng-composition:
(define (push-setting key value settings) (alist-cons key value settings))
(define (apply-profile overrides settings)
  (fold (lambda (o acc) (push-setting (car o) (cdr o) acc)) settings overrides))
(define final (apply-profile '((volume . 9) (theme . dark))
                             '((volume . 5) (theme . light) (lang . en))))
(display (list 'volume (cdr (assq 'volume final)) 'theme (cdr (assq 'theme final))
               'lang (cdr (assq 'lang final)) 'layers (length final)))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.math-composition:
(define (extend-graph x y g) (alist-cons x y g))
(define (graph-of proc xs)
  (fold (lambda (x acc) (extend-graph x (proc x) acc)) '() xs))
(define squares (graph-of (lambda (n) (* n n)) '(1 2 3 4)))
(display (list 'graph squares 'at-3 (cdr (assq 3 squares))))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.cs-composition:
(define (frame-bind name value env) (alist-cons name value env))
(define (visible env)
  (fold (lambda (p acc) (if (assq (car p) acc) acc (cons p acc))) '() env))
(define env (frame-bind 'x 3 (frame-bind 'y 2 (frame-bind 'x 1 '()))))
(display (list 'frames (length env) 'names (length (visible env)) 'x (cdr (assq 'x (visible env)))))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.base: alist-cons puts one labelled value in front of the rest and shares the tail.
row-5-emergence.emergent: eng: fold the one-setting push over a whole list of overrides and you have a profile system -- apply-profile never mentions alist-cons, it only calls push-setting, and the defaults survive underneath as a restorable layer. math: fold the same push over a range and you have materialised a function as data; the graph can now be searched, inverted or serialised, none of which you can do to a lambda. cs: fold it the other way, keeping only the first pair seen for each name, and you have computed which bindings are actually visible -- the shadowing that alist-cons created is now something the program can measure.
row-5-emergence.meta: The composition is alist-cons under a fold, three times, and the fold's seed is what changes the meaning: seeding with the defaults makes it an override stack, seeding with '() makes it a constructor, and folding over the RESULT instead makes it an analysis. The verb is one cons in all three; everything interesting is in what surrounds it.
row-5-emergence.eng: apply-profile is the whole feature and it is four lines, because pushing is associative-in-order: applying two profiles in sequence is the same as applying their concatenation.
row-5-emergence.math: Turning a procedure into its graph is the move that makes a function a first-class value you can inspect. It only terminates for a finite domain, which is why xs is a list and not a range.
row-5-emergence.cs: Counting visible names is how a compiler reports a shadowed variable warning. The information was already in the structure; the fold just reads it out.
